steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on Hilbert-Poincaré series of affine semi-regular polynomial sequences and the related Gröbner bases. Set up the notation, explain why the complexity of Gröbner basis computation matters, describe the survey part and the new results of the second part, and state the main theorem.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Notation (K, R, top part, homogenization, ideals, HF/HS) and Gröbner bases; MP/MQ problem and cryptography
- Gröbner basis algorithms and how their complexity is estimated
- First part of the paper: survey of Gröbner basis computation and its complexity
- Second part: affine semi-regular sequences, main theorem
- Application to reduced Gröbner bases

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Setup
  - K field, R=K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]
  - f^{\rm top}: maximal total degree part (top part); f^{h}: homogenization in R^{\prime}=R[y] (Subsection 3.1)
  - \langle F\rangle_{R} ideal generated by F; {\rm HF}_{M}, {\rm HS}_{M} Hilbert function / Hilbert–Poincaré series of graded module M
  - Gröbner basis: special generating set, computational tool for properties of I
  - MP problem: find common zero of f_{1},\ldots,f_{m} in K^{n}; all quadratic = MQ problem
  - MQ hardness -> public-key cryptosystems, digital signatures, expected quantum resistant
  - so complexity of Gröbner bases important in theory and practice
- Algorithms + complexity
  - Buchberger first; improvements F_{4}, F_{5} (summary in Subsection 3.1)
  - complexity hard in general; estimates via solving degree, degree of regularity, Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity, first/last fall degrees; relations surveyed elsewhere
- Part one (survey)
  - complexity for zero-dimensional ideals
  - Section 2: Koszul complex, Hilbert-Poincaré series, semi-regular sequence
  - Subsection 3.1: existing algorithms; Subsection 3.2: complexity of reduced Gröbner basis via homogenization
- Part two
  - affine (cryptographic) semi-regular: \bm{F}^{\rm top} (cryptographic) semi-regular (Definitions 4, 7, 8)
  - Pardue conjecture: homogeneous semi-regular = generic; affine ones common in multivariate cryptosystems / signatures
  - Section 4: relate HS of R^{\prime}/\langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle and R/\langle\bm{F}^{\rm top}\rangle; corollary: truncation at degree D-1, D degree of regularity
  - theorem: HF identity, equality of leading monomial ideals for d<D (DRL ordering), HS formula mod z^{D}, \bm{F}^{h} D -regular
- Application (Section 5)
  - reduced Gröbner bases of \langle\bm{F}\rangle, \langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle, \langle\bm{F}^{\rm top}\rangle; degree < D or not
  - rigorous proofs of existing results used in complexity analysis, extended to our case

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Let K be a field and let R=K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] be the polynomial ring in n variables over K. For a polynomial f in R, we write f^{\rm top} for its maximal total degree part, which we call the top part of f here, and f^{h} for its homogenization in R^{\prime}=R[y] with an extra variable y (details are in Subsection 3.1 below). The ideal generated by a non-empty subset F of R is denoted by \langle F\rangle_{R} (or simply \langle F\rangle). For a finitely generated graded R -(or R^{\prime} -)module M, we write {\rm HF}_{M} and {\rm HS}_{M} for its Hilbert function and its Hilbert–Poincaré series. A Gröbner basis of an ideal I in R is a special kind of generating set for I, and it is a computational tool to determine many properties of the ideal I. A typical application of computing Gröbner bases is to solve the multivariate polynomial (MP) problem: Given m polynomials f_{1},\ldots,f_{m} in R, find (a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})\in K^{n} such that f_{i}(a_{1},\ldots,a_{n})=0 for all i with 1\leq i\leq m. The particular case where all the polynomials are quadratic is called the MQ problem, and its hardness is used to construct public-key cryptosystems and digital signature schemes that are expected to be quantum resistant. So analyzing the complexity of computing Gröbner bases is one of the most important problems, both in theory and in practice.

The first algorithm for computing Gröbner bases was proposed by Buchberger, and since then a number of improvements of it have been proposed, like the F_{4} and F_{5} algorithms (Subsection 3.1 below gives a summary). It is very difficult in general to determine the complexity of computing Gröbner bases, but in some cases we can estimate it using several algebraic invariants, such as the solving degree, the degree of regularity, the Castelnuovo–Mumford regularity, and the first and last fall degrees; for the relations between these invariants we refer to another source.

The first part of this paper is a survey of Gröbner basis computation, and it reviews its complexity when the input polynomials generate a zero-dimensional ideal. For this, Section 2 first recalls foundations in commutative algebra like the Koszul complex, Hilbert-Poincaré series, and semi-regular sequences, which are useful for estimating the complexity of computing Gröbner bases. Then Subsection 3.1 gives an overview of existing Gröbner basis algorithms. After that, Subsection 3.2 describes how to estimate the complexity of computing the reduced Gröbner basis of a zero-dimensional ideal, using the notion of homogenization.

- Part two: affine semi-regular sequences
  - \bm{F} affine (cryptographic) semi-regular if \bm{F}^{\rm top} is (cryptographic) semi-regular (Definitions 4, 7, 8)
  - Pardue conjecture: homogeneous semi-regular sequences generic; affine ones common in multivariate cryptosystems / signature schemes
  - Section 4: relate HS of R^{\prime}/\langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle to R/\langle\bm{F}^{\rm top}\rangle; corollary: truncation at degree D-1
  - theorem statement (HF identity, LM ideals agree for d<D under DRL, HS mod z^{D}, \bm{F}^{h} D -regular)
- Application in Section 5
  - reduced Gröbner bases of \langle\bm{F}\rangle, \langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle, \langle\bm{F}^{\rm top}\rangle, degree < D or not
  - rigorous proofs of existing complexity results, extended to our case

The first part of this paper is a survey of Gröbner basis computation, and it reviews its complexity when the input polynomials generate a zero-dimensional ideal. For this, Section 2 first recalls foundations in commutative algebra like the Koszul complex, Hilbert-Poincaré series, and semi-regular sequences, which are useful for estimating the complexity of computing Gröbner bases. Then Subsection 3.1 gives an overview of existing Gröbner basis algorithms. After that, Subsection 3.2 describes how to estimate the complexity of computing the reduced Gröbner basis of a zero-dimensional ideal, using the notion of homogenization.

In the second part we focus on affine semi-regular polynomial sequences. A sequence \bm{F}=(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})\in R^{m} of (not necessarily homogeneous) polynomials is called affine (cryptographic) semi-regular if \bm{F}^{\rm top}=(f_{1}^{\rm top},\ldots,f_{m}^{\rm top}) is (cryptographic) semi-regular (see Definitions 4, 7, and 8 for details). Pardue conjectured that homogeneous semi-regular sequences are generic sequences of polynomials, and affine (cryptographic) semi-regular sequences often appear when multivariate public key cryptosystems and digital signature schemes are constructed. In Section 4 below we relate the Hilbert-Poincaré series of R^{\prime}/\langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle to that of R/\langle\bm{F}^{\rm top}\rangle. As a corollary we get an explicit formula for the truncation at degree D-1 of the Hilbert-Poincaré series of R^{\prime}/\langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle, where D is the degree of regularity for \langle\bm{F}^{\rm top}\rangle. These results are summarized in the following theorem:

With notation as above, assume that \bm{F} is affine cryptographic semi-regular. Then {\rm HF}_{R^{\prime}/\langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle}(d)=\sum_{i=0}^{d}{\rm HF}_{R/\langle\bm{F}^{\rm top}\rangle}(i) and (\langle\mathrm{LM}(\langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle)\rangle_{R^{\prime}})_{d}=(\langle\mathrm{LM}(\langle\bm{F}^{\rm top}\rangle)\rangle_{R^{\prime}})_{d} for each d with d<D, where a DRL ordering is used on the set of monomials in R and its homogenization on that in R^{\prime}. So we also get {\rm HS}_{R^{\prime}/\langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle}(z)\equiv\prod_{i=1}^{m}(1-z^{d_{i}})/(1-z)^{n+1}\pmod{z^{D}}, and so \bm{F}^{h} is D -regular (the definition of d -regularity is in Definition 4).

As an application of this theorem, in Section 5 below we explore reduced Gröbner bases of \langle\bm{F}\rangle, \langle\bm{F}^{h}\rangle, and \langle\bm{F}^{\rm top}\rangle, and we divide into the cases where the degree is less than D or not. In particular, we give rigorous proofs of some existing results that are often used for analyzing the complexity of computing Gröbner bases, and we also extend them to our case.
